slides.title: Outline
bullets: **Pipeline:** who enters academia and who stays
**Evaluation:** hiring, letters and promotion committees
**Funding:** grant success, award size and the role of reviewers
**Publishing and citations:** authorship, peer review, credit
**Pay, parenthood, teaching and service**
**Neuroscience** as a case study
**Interventions:** what has been tested and what worked
All sources, data and figures: github.com/jmourabarbosa/gender-bias

slides.title: 1. The pipeline
slides.sub: Who enters academia, who is promoted, who leaves

slides.title: In the EU, women earn 48% of PhDs but hold 30% of full professorships
slides.source: Source: European Commission, She Figures 2024, Fig. 6.1 (EU-27, 2019 and 2022). Grade A = full professor; grade C = entry-level post-PhD.

slides.title: In France, women's share of university professors doubled since 2000 but is still 33%
bullets: Women are **45%** of maîtres de conférences but **33%** of professors (2024)
Professors: 17% women in 2000, 23% in 2010
CNRS: women are 34.7% of researchers and **31.7%** of directeurs de recherche (2022)
Inserm: 66% of PhD students are women, 26% of the top research-director grade
slides.source: Sources: MESR, Vers l'égalité femmes-hommes ? Chiffres clés 2026, p. 36-40; CNRS Plan d'action égalité 2024-2026, p. 5; Inserm, Journée Inserm 2024 (parité).

slides.title: Women leave publishing science at a 19.5% higher yearly rate than men
bullets: Publication careers of 1.5 million scientists, 1955-2010
Yearly dropout: **10.8%** of women vs **9.0%** of men
Women's careers are shorter, so their lifetime output is lower
If dropout is equalized, the productivity gap shrinks from **27% to 9%**
slides.source: Source: Huang, Gates, Sinatra & Barabási (2020) PNAS 117:4609, Fig. 4. doi:10.1073/pnas.1914221117

slides.title: US women faculty are more likely than men to leave at every rank
bullets: Each year, women are **6%, 10% and 19%** more likely to leave as assistant, associate and full professors
Promotion rates are lower for women at the same seniority
Women more often report being **pushed out** by workplace climate, not pulled to better jobs
slides.source: Source: Spoon, LaBerge, Wapman et al. (2023) Science Advances 9:eadi2205, Fig. 1 (A attrition, B promotion). doi:10.1126/sciadv.adi2205

slides.title: Equal attrition alone will not bring US faculty to parity by 2060
bullets: Women: **46%** of US doctorates (2021), **36%** of tenure-track faculty
In 90% of fields, hiring shaped women's representation more than attrition (2011-2020)
Removing the attrition gap gives only a marginal gain
Parity needs sustained changes to **hiring**
slides.source: Source: LaBerge, Wapman, Clauset & Larremore (2024) eLife 13:RP93755, Fig. 3 (OA observed attrition, GNA gender-neutral attrition, IR/ER increasing/equal hiring). 268,769 faculty.

slides.title: 6. Neuroscience
slides.sub: Training, faculty, citations and conference talks

slides.title: In US neuroscience, women are 57% of PhD applicants but 30% of faculty
bullets: Women are **58%** of admitted students and 50% of postdocs (2016-17)
Faculty share has changed little in a decade
Women are **13.8%** of tenured full professors (2017-18)
Journals 2005-2017: 33.1% of first authors are women, **18.1%** of last authors
slides.source: Sources: SfN 2016-17 Neuroscience Departments & Programs Survey, executive summary; Machlovi et al. (2021) J Neurosci Res 99:9 (citing Bendels 2018, Shen 2018).

slides.title: Papers led by women are under-cited in cognitive neuroscience
bullets: J Cogn Neurosci 2009-2020: papers with men as first and last author (MM) are cited **+42%** above parity
Papers with women in both positions (WW) are cited **44%** below
Across neuro journals, women first/last authors rose from 36% (1995) to 50% (2018)
Yet the citation gap widens by 0.41 points per year
slides.source: Sources: Fulvio, Akinnola & Postle (2021) J Cogn Neurosci 33:3, Fig. 2 (Gender Citation Balance Index, bioRxiv version); Churchland & Davatolhagh (2024) The Transmitter, citing Dworkin et al. (2020).

slides.title: Women are a third of speakers at neuroscience meetings
bullets: BiasWatchNeuro, 676 meetings: **32.9%** of listed speakers are women
274 of 657 meetings fall below the field's own share of women
Major neuro conferences: women speakers rose from **24% to 42%** (2011-2019)
Brain stimulation conference: 2 women of 39 speakers (2015), 0 of 10 (2017)
slides.source: Sources: biaswatchneuro.com posts (scraped, data/biaswatchneuro.csv; year = post date); Else (2019) Nature 573:184; Hoy, Fitzgibbon & Brem (2021) eLife 10:e75818.

slides.title: Cosyne 2019 accepted 31% of abstracts with women first authors vs 38% for men
bullets: 83 of 264 woman-led abstracts accepted vs 255 of 677 man-led
Cosyne then moved to double-blind review; the gender gap did not close
Cosyne 2020 chairs guaranteed **50%** of podium talks to women
slides.source: Sources: C. Frye blog (6 Mar 2019), data from M. Carey; Simons Foundation SCGB (2020) 'Addressing gender and institutional bias at Cosyne'; UChicago Neuroscience Institute (2020).

slides.title: 2. Evaluation
slides.sub: Hiring, recommendation letters and promotion committees

slides.title: Faculty offered a 'female' lab manager applicant $3,700 less for the same CV
bullets: 127 science faculty rated one application, randomly named John or Jennifer
Mean salary offered: **$26,508** to Jennifer vs **$30,238** to John
Jennifer was also rated less competent and hireable, and offered less mentoring
Women faculty showed the same bias as men
slides.source: Source: Moss-Racusin et al. (2012) PNAS 109:16474, Fig. 2. doi:10.1073/pnas.1211286109

slides.title: For tenure-track jobs, faculty preferred a woman 2:1 over an equal man
bullets: 873 faculty chose between identical, highly qualified candidates
Women ranked first by **67%** of faculty, in biology, engineering and psychology
Exception: male economists showed no preference
slides.source: Source: Williams & Ceci (2015) PNAS 112:5360, Fig. 1. doi:10.1073/pnas.1418878112

slides.title: CNRS committees with implicit bias promoted fewer women, but only when they denied that bias exists
bullets: 40 CNRS promotion committees (414 members), all disciplines, over 2 years
Most committee members held an implicit 'science = male' association
Year 2 (no reminder of the study): committees with stronger implicit bias promoted **fewer women**
This happened only in committees that **did not believe** women face external barriers
Committees that acknowledged barriers showed no link between implicit bias and decisions
Source: Régner, Thinus-Blanc, Netter, Schmader & Huguet (2019) Nature Human Behaviour 3:1171. doi:10.1038/s41562-019-0686-3

slides.title: Recommendation letters call women 'excellent' less often than men
bullets: Geoscience postdoc letters: **15%** excellent for women vs **24%** for men
Faculty-job letters use more standout adjectives for men (0.70 vs 0.60 per letter)
Letters describe women as more communal and less agentic
Papers by two women authors use positive self-descriptions 12.3% less often
slides.source: Sources: Dutt et al. (2016) Nature Geoscience 9:805, Table 4; Schmader, Whitehead & Wysocki (2007) Sex Roles 57:509; Madera, Hebl & Martin (2009) J Appl Psychol 94:1591; Lerchenmueller, Sorenson & Jena (2019) BMJ 367:l6573.

slides.title: 3. Funding
slides.sub: Success rates, award sizes and what reviewers evaluate

slides.title: Sweden 1995: women needed 64 extra impact points to score as competent as men
bullets: Swedish Medical Research Council postdoc fellowships
Equivalent to about **3 extra Nature or Science papers**
Being affiliated with a reviewer also raised scores
A UK Wellcome follow-up found no gap (27.5% vs 26.9% success)
slides.source: Sources: Wennerås & Wold (1997) Nature 387:341, Table 1 (redrawn); Grant, Burden & Breen (1997) Nature 390:438 (not verified, paywalled).

slides.title: Gaps appear when reviewers judge the applicant, not the science
bullets: Canadian Institutes of Health Research, 23,918 applications
When review focused on the science, women's success gap was **0.9 points**
When review focused on the investigator, it was **4.0 points**
slides.source: Source: Witteman, Hendricks, Straus & Tannenbaum (2019) Lancet 393:531, Fig. 1 (bioRxiv preprint version).

slides.title: On average, grant success gaps are small; award sizes differ more
bullets: Meta-analysis of 21 studies: men have **7%** higher odds of funding
Meta-analysis 2005-2020: award rates **1 point** apart, but women receive smaller awards
Dutch NWO Veni: 14.9% vs 17.7% success (finding later contested)
NIH R01 name-swap experiment: no bias against women or Black PIs
Gates Foundation, blinded review: women scored lower, explained by word choice
NIH: once funded, women keep funding as long as men

Sources: Bornmann et al. 2007 J Informetrics; Schmaling & Gallo 2023 Res Integr Peer Rev; van der Lee & Ellemers 2015 PNAS; Forscher et al. 2019 Nat Hum Behav; Kolev et al. 2019 NBER w25759; Hechtman et al. 2018 PNAS

slides.title: First-time NIH grants to women are a median $39,000 smaller
bullets: Median first award: **$126,615** to women vs **$165,721** to men
Gap is largest at Big Ten universities
Start-up packages for junior biomedical faculty: **$350k** vs **$889k** median
slides.source: Sources: Oliveira, Ma, Woodruff & Uzzi (2019) JAMA 321:898, Table 2 (redrawn); Sege, Nykiel-Bub & Selk (2015) JAMA 314:1175 (from press release).

slides.title: ERC: women won 44% of Starting Grants (2024) but 23.5% of Advanced Grants (2023)
bullets: Starting Grant share rose from about 25% in 2007
Advanced Grant share peaked at 27.5% in 2022
Starting Grant success rates differ by 0.5 to 1 point by gender
France ANR 2024: 26% success for women vs 24% for men
slides.source: Sources: ERC results via EU-Büro (German national contact point) and Times Higher Education (data/erc_women_share_grantees.csv); Jesus-Rydin et al. EGU24-16168; ANR (2026) Femmes et hommes dans l'AAPG 2015-2025.

slides.title: 4. Publishing and citations
slides.sub: Authorship, peer review, credit and recognition

slides.title: Women are 13% less likely than men to be named as authors on their team's papers
bullets: Linked US administrative data on 9,778 research teams
Gap: **13%** for articles, **58%** for patents
Women's actual share of authorships falls below their share of potential authorships at every career stage
Physics last authors: about **258 years** to parity at current rates
slides.source: Sources: Ross et al. (2022) Nature 608:135, Fig. 1; Holman, Stuart-Fox & Hauser (2018) PLoS Biol 16:e2004956.

slides.title: Women write 37% of papers but do 28% of reviews and 26% of editing
bullets: Frontiers journals, contributions up to 2015
Editors of both genders favour reviewers of their own gender
AGU journals: women are 20% of reviewers vs 27% of first authors
Editorial outcomes: no penalty for women across 145 journals
slides.source: Sources: Helmer et al. (2017) eLife 6:e21718, Fig. 1; Lerback & Hanson (2017) Nature 541:455; Squazzoni et al. (2021) Science Advances 7:eabd0299.

slides.title: In early COVID-19, women's share of first authorships fell 23% below expected
bullets: COVID-19 medical papers in 2020 vs the same journals in 2019
medRxiv: women first authors fell from 34% to 22% (Mar-Apr 2019 vs 2020)
Scientists with a child under 5 lost **17% more** research time
slides.source: Sources: Andersen et al. (2020) eLife 9:e58807, Fig. 1; Vincent-Lamarre, Sugimoto & Larivière (2020) Nature Index; Myers et al. (2020) Nat Hum Behav 4:880.

slides.title: Neuroscience papers by two women are cited 13.9% less than expected
bullets: Reference lists in 5 top neuroscience journals, 1995-2018
Man first and last author: cited **+5.2%** above expected
Woman first and last author: **-13.9%**
The imbalance comes mostly from reference lists of men-led papers
Medicine: median 33 citations for women-led vs 59 for men-led papers
slides.source: Sources: Dworkin et al. (2020) Nature Neuroscience 23:918, Fig. 2 (bioRxiv version); Chatterjee & Werner (2021) JAMA Netw Open 4:e2114509, Table 3.

slides.title: Women won 19% of top research awards in 2016-2020, below their share of professors
bullets: 141 prestigious international awards, 2001-2020: women won **11.5%**
Share rose from 6% to 19%
Biomedical prizes: women receive **64 cents** per dollar men receive
Men self-cite **56%** more than women
slides.source: Sources: Meho (2021) Quantitative Science Studies 2:976, Fig. 2; Ma, Oliveira, Woodruff & Uzzi (2019) Nature 565:287; King et al. (2017) Socius 3.

slides.title: At seminars, men are 2.5 times more likely than women to ask a question
bullets: 247 seminars at 35 institutions
Women ask fewer questions than their share of the audience
US colloquium speakers: **69%** men; 49% women when a woman chairs, 30% when a man does
Nature news quotes from women rose from 13% (2005) to 31% (2020)
slides.source: Sources: Carter et al. (2018) PLoS ONE 13:e0202743, Fig. 1; Nittrouer et al. (2018) PNAS 115:104; Davidson & Greene (2024) eLife 12:e84855.

slides.title: 5. Pay, parenthood, teaching and service
US women faculty earn 83.6% of men's average salary
bullets: Gap persists within every rank (2025-26)
UK higher education: median gap **11.5%** (2023-24)
CNRS: women earn **13.9%** less, about €557 per month (2021)
Inserm: 13.1% gap for permanent staff
slides.source: Sources: AAUP Annual Report on the Economic Status of the Profession 2025-26, Fig. 2; UCEA Intersectional Pay Gaps 2023-24; CNRS MPDF pay analysis (2023); Inserm (2024).

slides.title: 43% of new mothers in STEM left full-time STEM work, vs 23% of new fathers
bullets: US scientists followed 2003-2010 after their first child
Mothers' publication output drops by 17% to 48% after a first child, depending on field
1950s-60s US scientists: **27%** of mothers vs **48%** of fathers got tenure
slides.source: Sources: Cech & Blair-Loy (2019) PNAS 116:4182, Fig. 1 (fathers shown); Morgan et al. (2021) Science Advances 7:eabd1996; Kim & Moser (2021) NBER w29436.

slides.title: Students rated the same online instructor lower when told she was a woman
bullets: Two instructors swapped names in an online course
Same grading turnaround: promptness **4.35** vs **3.55**
Sciences Po: male students were 33% more likely to rate men 'excellent', not linked to exam results
Maastricht: women rated lower, mostly junior women
slides.source: Sources: MacNell, Driscoll & Hunt (2015) Innov High Educ 40:291 (from press release); Boring (2017) J Public Econ 145:27; Mengel, Sauermann & Zölitz (2019) JEEA 17:535.

slides.title: Women accept 76% of requests for low-promotability tasks, men 51%
bullets: Asked to volunteer, women say yes more often; unasked, rates are equal
US faculty: women do **0.6 h/week** more service
Associate professors: women spend 25% of time on research vs 37% for men
slides.source: Sources: Babcock, Recalde, Vesterlund & Weingart (2017) AER 107:714, Exp. 3; Guarino & Borden (2017) Res High Educ 58:672; Misra et al. (2011) Academe 97(1).

slides.title: 7. Interventions
slides.sub: What has been tested, and how strong the evidence is

slides.title: The famous blind-audition result does not survive a correction for multiple tests
bullets: Goldin & Rouse: screens raised women's chances in preliminary rounds by **11 points**
That estimate had p = 0.042; Bonferroni-corrected across 8 tests, p = 0.33
Gelman: the evidence is 'not very impressive'
slides.source: Sources: Goldin & Rouse (2000) AER 90:715, Table 5; Pallesen (2019) 'Orchestrating false beliefs about gender discrimination'; Gelman via Reason (2019).

slides.title: Double-blind review cuts prestige bias; effects on women are mixed
bullets: WSDM 2017: single-blind reviewers favoured famous authors (OR **1.63**) and top institutions
Women authors: OR 0.78, confidence interval includes 1
Behavioral Ecology: double-blind review did not raise women's first authorship
Cosyne: double-blind review did not close the gap
slides.source: Sources: Tomkins, Zhang & Heavlin (2017) PNAS 114:12708, Table 5 (redrawn); Cox & Montgomerie (2019) PeerJ 7:e6702.

slides.title: A bias habit-breaking workshop raised women's share of new hires from 32% to 47%
bullets: Cluster-randomized trial in 92 University of Wisconsin departments
Bias awareness rose at 3 months
Control departments went from 33% to 32%
Few hires per department, so the estimate is noisy
slides.source: Sources: Carnes et al. (2015) Acad Med 90:221; Devine et al. (2017) J Exp Soc Psychol 73:211 (OSF preprint).

slides.title: Gender-neutral tenure-clock stopping helped men, not women
bullets: Top-50 US economics departments: men's tenure rate rose, women's fell (working-paper estimates)
More women on promotion committees did not raise women's success (Spain, Italy)
Athena SWAN (UK): women professors 24.2% to 26.8%
ERC: eligibility extended 18 months per child
Review of grant-review interventions: 1 tested study in 5,524 records
slides.source: Sources: Antecol, Bedard & Stearns (2018) AER 108:2420 (IZA DP 9904 values); Bagues et al. (2017) AER 107:1207; Xiao et al. (2020) BMJ Open; ERC Work Programme 2026; Tricco et al. (2017) PLoS ONE.

slides.title: Summary
bullets: Women reach parity at the PhD but are fewer at each later stage; hiring and higher attrition both contribute
Controlled experiments show bias in how applicants are judged, but hiring results are mixed
Funding gaps are small in success rates and larger in award size and investigator-focused review
Women receive less credit: authorship, citations, prizes and speaking slots
Parenthood and service load fall more on women
Few interventions have strong evidence, and some policies backfired
Sources, data and figures: github.com/jmourabarbosa/gender-bias
